“Tell me I’ve lived a good life. Tell me I’m a good man” Someone else said Saving Private Ryan works for a metaphor as US involvement in wars in general, in the sense that there’s always a private Ryan to save, a cause to fight for, and the sacrifice made will always be greater than the life saved. In trying to convince the audience that this great sacrifice is the point of war or why it’s necessary, the film misses the fact that this is precisely why war is irredeemably pointless. The film wants to portray all our lead heroes as victims of brutality who want it to end, but also encourages them to be perpetrators of brutality. Upham is the best example of this. He starts the film as a staunch pacifist, someone who wants to bring an end to the brutality on both sides through strict adherence to the Geneva conventions. By the end of the film however, motivated by revenge, he gives into his rage and kills a surrendered German soldier, starting the cycle of violence and brutality once again. The film frames this loss of empathy as heroic. None of my issues with the film are in the directing/filmmaking of it. Spielberg is great and he’s really firing off all cylinders here. But none of that matters (in fact it might make it worse) if the script that directing is supporting creates a world where war is always justified as long as you have a private to save.

I just watched this movie for the first time in 30 years. And while the film is nothing short of an astounding technical achievement, it is as morally and philosophically bankrupt as a film like this could possibly be. ﻿ ﻿Setting aside the events that led up to D-Day and the US entry into a two-front war, this film makes two arguments that I find absolutely appalling: ﻿ ﻿1) That a pacifist subjected to the horrors of war can be thus justified in the committing of a cold-blooded murder. ﻿2) That all who come after owe it to those who gave their lives to be better people because of their sacrifice. ﻿ ﻿When the Captain says "Earn this" to Ryan, I thought that was a really lousy thing to do to another human being. The plot had already established that not only had Ryan had no say in the mission, he vehemently disagreed with it, and wanted nothing to do with it. So for the captain to say that is to put a burden on Ryan that he in no way deserved. ﻿ ﻿But that isn't even the point of that line. Spielberg is trying to tell all of us that we owe it to those who died to earn their sacrifice. And while one can certainly commend them for ending the tyranny of the Nazis, that doesn't mean we all owe it to them to live the lives that they did not get to. Their sacrifice was in the name of freedom. To me, this film seems to make the argument that the sacrifice was in the name of war. ﻿ ﻿Captain Miller could have died anywhere in Europe. He and his team could have died on Omaha Beach. But because they died on that bridge, that doesn't make Private Ryan indebted to them for a sacrifice he did not ask for. And to see a broken old man on that beach 50 years later asking his wife for validation is just piling on. ﻿ ﻿And Upham's murder of the German soldier he previously campaigned to release is somehow meant to show that the horrors of war can change even the least warlike of men. But the manner in which this happens is in purely cold blood, as justification for Upham watching him shoot the captain. Upham has a perfect position to fire his weapon in combat, and the movie could have done that. Instead, Upham takes the prisoners, and shoots the one in cold blood. ﻿ ﻿Nothing justifies this murder. We are meant to see Upham reshaped by war, but to what end? That murder is justified in some context? Upham's lack of remorse in his action contributes to the idea that Spielberg is saying the murder is justified, but I don't agree. ﻿ ﻿I left the movie feeling very unsettled. There's a lot of emotional manipulation here, and a lot of scenes that ring very hollow thirty years later. And while this may be a strong technical achievement, as a film - as a work of art - I find it lacking.

Saving Private Ryan is a technically phenomenal war movie that constantly wants to convince you how horrible war is while simultaneously making it fucking exciting. The Normandy landing is the perfect example: Spielberg throws you into an almost unbearably brutal depiction of chaos, mutilation and death, but the sound design, camerawork and sheer kinetic energy make the whole thing incredibly thrilling. That’s ultimately what sticks with me more than Tom Hanks explaining how the war changed him. Spielberg wants to horrify you and thrill you at the same time, and I’m not sure he ever completely reconciles those two impulses. That contradiction becomes even more apparent in the movie’s treatment of its soldiers. The Americans get individual long deaths, fear, pain and humanity, while German soldiers are usually reduced to targets who get shot and then fall down like a sack of potatoes. This isn’t about pretending German soldiers were innocent, or about equating their suffering with that of the people they were fighting against. The war against Nazi Germany had a legitimate and necessary cause. But the average German soldier was still a human being rather than an interchangeable Nazi monster, and the film rarely seems interested in that distinction. The sniper is the clearest example: he’s not just competent, he’s framed as almost divinely righteous, constantly associated with his cross and his faith. The film wants the violence to feel brutally realistic while still surrounding its American soldiers with an almost mythological layer of heroism and righteousness. Maybe Spielberg is simply the wrong director for this particular kind of war movie. His sentimentality works beautifully when the moral framework is this clear—Schindler’s List, E.T., and many of his other films thrive on that emotional directness. But Saving Private Ryan wants to examine the physical and moral ugliness of war while filtering it through a very American language of sacrifice, family, faith and heroism. This is especially understandable considering that Spielberg made the film partly as a tribute to his father, a World War II veteran whose stories had shaped his lifelong fascination with the war. But that personal connection may also explain why the film ultimately feels less interested in the universal tragedy of war than in honoring the generation of Americans who fought it. The most interesting contradiction comes from the film’s central moral question. Why should eight men risk their lives to save one? The obvious answer seems to be that human life cannot simply be reduced to arithmetic: one life isn’t worth less than eight. Yet the ending quietly asks us to do exactly that calculation again. Ryan stands in front of Miller’s grave with his family behind him, and the film shows us the life that resulted from the sacrifice: his children, grandchildren, an entire family. “Tell me I’ve lived a good life. Tell me I’m a good man.” It’s emotionally powerful, but the imagery effectively tells us that the sacrifice was worthwhile because of everything that came after it. The film starts by rejecting the idea that lives can be weighed against one another, then ends by giving us a very sentimental reason why perhaps this particular life was worth the price. And honestly, after the Normandy sequence, I found the film increasingly exhausting. The characters are mostly archetypes rather than people I became deeply attached to, and the endless procession of battles and moral speeches started to feel repetitive. Also nothing came even close to the beginning of the movie. Platoon, for me, leaves behind the feeling of people being psychologically and morally destroyed by war; Saving Private Ryan leaves behind images of one incredibly well-made battle. It’s a remarkable piece of filmmaking, and I completely understand why its patriotic sentimentality resonates with so many people. But for a film that wants to show us what war really is, I wish Spielberg had been willing to look beyond the heroism, sacrifice and emotional reassurance that he is so naturally drawn to.

*SPOILERS* A technical landmark, but a deeply incoherent one. Saving Private Ryan doesn't need to preach or pick a side, but it does need to remain coherent. It tries to play both ends of the spectrum - treating war as a senseless, dehumanising nightmare while simultaneously running on classic Hollywood emotional manipulation. The result isn't a complex look at conflict; it's just tonal whiplash. This lack of coherence completely unravels in the third act. Mellish’s death in the attic isn't raw realism - it's a heavily stylized, cinematic set-piece designed to milk maximum dread out of the viewer. Upham’s later "revenge" execution of that same German soldier totally breaks the film's internal logic. Framing his action as some triumphant moment of resolve doesn't undo the tragedy in that room, nor does it deliver actual catharsis. It’s just cheap narrative patching to give the audience an easy win where none belongs. Framing the entire film with a golden-hued, flag-waving cemetery sequence at the start and end only underlines how incoherent it really is. You can't ground a movie in gritty, visceral spectacle and then force it into a tidy, patriotic box. It isn't a nuanced take on the reality of war - it’s just a film constantly at odds with its own structure. Sorry, I know I have a lot of beef with this film.

"It's quite a few." "Yes it is. Quite a few." Endlessly frustrating movie. Of course, there's the oft-discussed imbalance between Spielberg's stringently brutal formal construction and war-is-hell sequencing and the film's interminable flag-waving patriotics, but there's also the more pressing issue surrounding the film's core thesis: Ryan is not a man, he is America. He is the emblem of his nation's values and the poster child for the young American military success story. The penultimate bridge scene offers a genuinely earnest chance for The Great American War Movie to finally divert from convention and not salute American ideals so much give them a responsibility to live up to those who have died in the name of service to their country. When a dying and battle-weary Tom Hanks paused in-between losing pints of blood to whisper "Earn this" into a fresh-faced Matt Damon's ear (who manages to maintain a steady skincare regiment despite having been airdropped into Nazi occupied France for the better part of a month), it wasn't simply a dying man's last wish or a vaguely sentimental gesture between captain and private. It was an order; a pledge to live by and die having seen through to its fullest. But then, Spielberg promptly discards that potentially introspective idea in the span of a Zemeckis-style CG scene transition, by having an aged and well-worn Ryan kneel at the graves of his fallen comrades, nearing the end of his life, and tearfully state that he has tried his utmost to honour their memory, shortly before seeking reassurance and comfort from his lovingly devoted wife. The bitter irony of it all ends up being that this (unassailably well made) wartime epic which centralises the hellishness of warfare and the toll it takes on those who fight it shies away from administering any true burden of responsibility upon a nation that so willingly and frequently throughout history dispensed of the lives of those who it claims to honour and owe to unendingly, in favour of self-congratulatory sentimentalism. War did not start and end with World War 2, and neither should the American pledge.

He designs the experience from the camera on, he decides what you have to look at, what you have to feel. He's like a big mum bird digesting the food for you and spitting it in your mouth. To me this is insulting. This one-fits-all experience of cinema as a mass event in which everyone sees the same thing, and feels the same thing horrifies me. That’s where my praise ends for this movie. It’s a war movie but what war movies always get wrong is that patriotism/nationalism has no place in a war movie. It cheapens the horrors of war when this movie tries to have its cake and eat it too. It wants to say, “isn’t this horrible how so many people are needlessly dying?” But simultaneously makes it seem like the American troops are the heroes. I get that WWII is sort of a layup in that America was fighting true atrocities, but war movies love to gloss over the innocents from the opposition to instead focus on the militants from the “good side”. We see people kill enemies that have surrendered and disregard for civilians from Tom Hank’s troop. I think the only good war movie can be an anti-war movie which is not this movie. It glorifies war but wants to act like it shows how atrocious war is at the same time which makes it fail overall. But goddamn I love Tom Hanks and would be lying if the movie wasn’t solidly made and acted which earns it a three star rating despite my major flaws and concerns with the movie. Steven Spielberg’s Saving Private Ryan is a structurally interesting war film, and features several exceptional moments throughout but also some highly conventional war tropes and a weak plot which make the message of the film a little difficult to take at face value. Firstly, the film features one of the most iconic war sequences in film history, featuring flawless kinetic handheld cinematography and epic uses of quick zoom ins and camera movements, perfectly encapsulating the horrors of war. However, after that groundbreaking intro, I feel the film really loses its momentum rapidly. It evolves from a revolutionary war epic to a highly conventional and unoriginal war story, relying overly on traditional sentimentality (especially at the finale) and predictable war tropes. While the film throughout still continues to use groundbreaking techniques, it feels like a significant diminish in originality, making it feel quite generic overall, However despite its unoriginal plot, it still remains an highly impressive technical feat in cinematic history.

I put this on during a flight from Europe thinking that I would watch the first half hour — a terrific and terrifically horrifying sequence of the Allied landing on Normandy — and then turn it off. But this time I was fascinated by the incredibly weird treatment of gender and watched it all the way through. The most striking scene in this respect is when the group of soldiers searching for Ryan are sitting in an abandoned church, lit only by candles, talking about their mothers. Borderline schmalzy and uncanny, this scene anticipates the *extremely* schmalzy closing scene, set decades in the future, when the now-aged Ryan tearfully asks his equally aged wife, “Am I a good man? Did I lead a good life?” Jeez guy please answer these questions for yourself. Women in this film exist only to be the passive foils of men, whether as bereaved mothers or supportive wives. The closest thing to an actual female character is a young French girl, maybe five years old, who is stranded in a bombed out building with her family. Her desperate father throws her down from above into the hands of one of the group of soldiers. After a fire fight, while the girl cowers among the soldiers, she is passed back to her father and the soldiers move on. The lesson here is that this world is an exclusively male one. Emotional complexity exists only among the men, whose relationships are at once fraternal, or father-son, or strangely erotic, with a tremendous sense of bodily intimacy. A very strange movie. Again, the terrible schmalzy ending is a huge misstep, much like the amazingly awkward ending of Schindler’s List. How you could make Jaws and then make those two is beyond me.

Saving Private Ryan should be relegated to the category of okay movie. After almost thirty years since my original viewing, it is hard to remember why this film was so lauded. I remember as a kid the theater being completely silent when it concluded, patrons with heads hung low, shuffling out in remembrance of what was lost and won. In retrospect it seems like it received such critical praise and accolades because the greatest generation was dying off and guilt did the rest of the work. Somehow Spielberg won Best Directing over Terrence Malick's The Thin Red Line, released the same year and a better film by every measure. I will give Saving Private Ryan Best Sound, Sound Editing, and Cinematography, but none of those awards require Spielberg. He directed a boring story that generates so much momentum in the first twenty minutes from the iconic D-Day landing that the energy alone carries you across the finish line. The rest of the film is a ragtag bunch of Rangers looking for Private Ryan, and just like Tom Hanks' squad asking why they are hunting for him, I too was wondering why this movie deserves praise for a boring fetch quest with no compelling answer as to why anyone cares about Ryan outside of his mother. The acting ranges from meh to okay. Part of the problem is Spielberg created tropes for characters. None of them felt real. The Rudy character as a scared soldier with a heart of gold, the rough around the edges guy from Brooklyn who means well once you get to know him. Maybe my age or internet-saturated storytelling has ruined my patience for this, but they mostly felt one-dimensional and wooden with zero character development across the entire runtime. My biggest gripe is the ending, which plays like a video game. Characters have plot armor that lets them run through bullets fired from fifty different Nazis, artillery strikes, and flak cannons without a scratch, unless the plot demands otherwise. About ten Americans with limited resources take on a battalion of Nazis with multiple tanks in their own WWII Battle of Thermopylae, fighting over a bridge that could be repaired in a week but is somehow of vital importance. The most egregious part is that each main American soldier kills approximately fifty Nazis apiece, as hoards of Germans seek out American bullets like moths to a flame. I was rolling my eyes. Bad writing, bad directing, and I am scratching my head as to why this was considered good even by 1998 standards. Saving Private Ryan is the cinematic equivalent of the books your English teacher forced you to read in high school. The same false arbiters of culture who decided Wuthering Heights and Slaughterhouse-Five must be preserved for future generations have decided this film is sacred. Saving Private Ryan is patriotism bordering on jingoism dressed up as prestige cinema.

Spielberg works his magic once again. The first 30 minutes or so of this film are masterfully shot, written, acted, and edited. It’s a genuinely unflinching, brutal, and deeply heartbreaking depiction of World War II that I have not seen anything like. The pain, the horror of it all, is ridiculously intense and it really puts things into perspective. The cinematography throughout is absolutely breathtaking, using natural landscapes, framing, and camera motion to perfectly capture the various emotions of the film. Tom Hanks delivers the standout performance here. I grow continually more impressed with his acting range and how he is able to portray such complex characters so well. Matt Damon is also great, as usual, and the supporting cast in general is very good as well. The storyline is extremely compelling (bring Matt Damon home 🤯) and results in an emotional, epic journey for a small squad of soldiers searching for one man. It truly feels like an epic journey in so many ways. I wouldn’t have minded if it was maybe just a half-hour shorter, as I found some of the really powerful moments not to be the loud, chaotic combat scenes, but the smaller-scale, intense interactions between soldiers just trying to keep surviving and getting through these traumatic experiences. There is a great amount of both, but my only real complaint with this movie is that it feels a bit long in parts. However, that’s a small nitpick in what is otherwise a ridiculously entertaining, important film that is masterfully made. There’s a reason that Spielberg is considered one of the best to ever do it. His range as a director is simply remarkable. He can create lighthearted, family friendly crowd pleasers like ET and then turn around and deliver a haunting, gorgeously shot war epic that captures the horrors of World War II.

This was such an easy 5 stars before some truly baffling creative decisions. The crude humor during moments of genuine mortal tension repeatedly pulled me out of the film. I understand what the characterization of Upham is doing and why he behaves the way he does, but frankly, I couldn’t care less. Everything about him repulsed me: the cowardice, the naïveté, his constant glorification of war, and especially the fact that he repeats what the film itself frames as a mistake by releasing more prisoners. And why have Steamboat come back? What exactly was the message there? Was it to suggest that you shouldn’t spare your enemies? That good deeds sometimes don’t go unpunished? Or that you should continue doing good despite that possibility? If it was the latter, I don’t think the film communicates it particularly well. And that’s what makes this so frustrating. This is still a fantastic movie. I had a genuinely great time watching it. Tom Hanks is stellar as ever, the plot is compelling, and the cinematography and action sequences are incredible. But man, I genuinely can’t remember the last time a film irritated me this much.

Por Santiago Lebrija (20 de septiembre de 1998) Steven Spielberg se ha consagrado en el corazón de niños y adultos en diferentes décadas. Cuando salió E.T., todos los niños de los 80 entendimos poco la película, pero quedamos conmovidos por la sensibilidad de Drew Barrymore y el perfecto extraterrestre que se quedó en la mente de todos. No obstante, a finales de los 80 y principios de los 90, con la trilogía de Indiana Jones, Jurassic Park, entre otros, atrajo a un público adulto que le gusta recordar su niñez desde otro punto de vista. Pero el maduro y veterano director necesitaba un Óscar en su carrera cinematográfica y decidió hacer una película cruda y a la vez conmovedora: creó La lista de Schindler, que le valió el Óscar como mejor director. Con aquel justo, esperado y merecido reconocimiento de parte de los miembros de la academia, Spielberg crece su imperio y cualquier producción que llevara su nombre impreso era un éxito en la taquilla, incluso una animación para la televisión para el canal Warner llamada Freakazoid, era producida por él. Lejos de la silla de director, Steven Spielberg vuelve a llevar a cabo una historia sobre la Segunda Guerra Mundial en la que esta vez incluye a Tom Hanks en el reparto, consagrado ya como un icono nacional, con la facilidad de sensibilizar hasta a Bob Dole. Como diría Octavio Paz, “la vida es un constante riesgo. Vivir es exponerse”. Esa misma es la propuesta de Spielberg para su versión de Salvando al soldado Ryan, que trata acerca de la misión de nueve hombres, dirigidos por Tom Hanks, que buscan a un soldado en particular, que ha perdido a sus tres hermanos en la guerra y a cuya madre ya le han avisado acerca de la muerte de sus hijos. En la búsqueda del soldado Ryan, el pelotón de rescate se encuentra con varios percances en el camino y poco a poco los hombres van muriendo y el resto del pelotón se empieza a desmoronar moralmente, sin mencionar que antes de esta peligrosa misión desembarcaron en Normandía y perdieron a la mitad de sus compañeros. La pregunta constante es si vale la pena arriesgar la vida de 9 o más hombres por uno, pero eso no pueden decidirlo ellos, ya que las órdenes son superiores. Esta es una de las películas más interesantes del director de Tiburón, y la impresionante dedicación y limpieza que le da al comienzo del film es de admirarse. Aunque poco a poco la cinta pierda fuerza, debido a la impactante introducción, se va enriqueciendo conforme los personajes van desapareciendo hasta llegar al climático punto en donde encuentran al soldado Ryan y la batalla que enfrentan. Sin embargo, no podía faltar ese falso orgullo nacionalista de los gringos, en donde imprimen una farsa sobre los valores norteamericanos, que desaparecieron hace tiempo, y el puritanismo y bondad del personaje de Tom Hanks, que cada que puede aprovecha para hacer aburridos, moralistas y nostálgicos discursos sobre la vida. Con esto no quiero demeritar la actuación del dos veces ganador del Óscar, sino confrontar esos absurdos sermones que pudieron haberse evitado para no destrozar el realismo del film. La película es buena y vale la pena verla, ya que tiene unas de las escenas más reales que se hayan filmado, y me atrevo a decir que está a la altura de películas de culto como Pelotón, de Oliver Stone, y Cara de guerra, de Stanley Kubrick; y aunque dije que está a la altura, no me atrevería a ponerla en el mismo nivel debido al discurso interno de cada film y el contenido intelectual de los dos mencionados films acerca de las guerras. Sin duda alguna, esta película estará nominada para varios Óscares.

The sheer scale Spielberg manages to convey is immense.

That opening battle might be one of the most insane things I’ve ever watched. Spielberg doesn’t make D-Day look exciting or heroic in the normal movie sense. People are drowning before they even reach the beach, bullets are ripping through soldiers, explosions make Miller temporarily lose his hearing, and medics are trying to save people who are already basically dead. The shaky camera, washed-out look, sound, and complete confusion make it feel like Spielberg is dropping you into the middle of Omaha Beach instead of letting you comfortably watch it. What surprised me is that the rest of the movie is much quieter. The mission to save Ryan sounds heroic until the soldiers start questioning why eight men should risk their lives for one person they don’t even know. Tom Hanks is perfect as Miller because he never feels like some unstoppable war hero. He’s exhausted, scared, his hand won’t stop shaking, and he’s just trying to keep his men together long enough to finish the mission. Wade’s death and Mellish getting slowly stabbed were especially hard to watch. I do think the movie loses a little momentum between the opening and final battle, but when that last battle starts Spielberg somehow manages to make everything feel chaotic while still letting me understand where everyone is and what they’re trying to do. “Earn this” is such a brutal thing for Ryan to have to carry for the rest of his life. After *Schindler’s List* and now this, Spielberg might be even better when he takes away all the spectacle and forces you to look directly at people.

A forma como Spielberg retrata a guerra é tão realista e intimista que mostra que os soldados não são heróis invencíveis, mas humanos. A cena mais memorável, pra mim, é o momento em que, antes de acontecer o ataque mais violento do filme, os soldados restantes ouvem  e cantam "Tu est partout", da Édith Piaf, em um gramofone improvisado no meio das ruínas. Isso humaniza eles, de certa forma, e rompe com o silêncio opressivo antes do ataque. Eles meio que deixam de serem soldados e voltam a serem civis, com famílias, casas, sonhos. Além disso, a cena em que Upham fica travado na escada no dilema de subir ou não, por mais que possa dar ao público um ar de covardia vindo do tradutor, é extremamente realista. Diante de soldados corajosos e acostumados com o caos da guerra, Upham representava a inocência do grupo, tendo até defendido um soldado alemão antes. A paralisia ao entregar as munições enquanto um americano morria no andar de cima mostra que Spielberg desmitifica o heroísmo de todos os soldados da guerra, retratando também o medo. A reação de Upham representa, mesmo que estressando o público, a reação mais provável e humana de um civil jogado em um combate. Eu até lembrei, na hora, do Dae-Ho, em Squid Game, que tem uma reação idêntica à essa, ficando paralisado e em pânico ao ter que entregar as munições ao grupo durante a rebelião. Uma reação completamente humana. Por fim, a reação de Upham acaba o humilhando, quando os soldados alemães passam por ele e nem atacam, mostrando que eles não o vêem como uma ameaça. E o desfecho é que ele acaba cometendo um crime de guerra, matando o soldado alemçao que ele mesmo havia insistido pra ficar, como forma de vingança ao Capitão Miller. Spielberg mostra como a guerra corrompe, até mesmo a pessoa mais inocente do grupo. A guerra tira a humanidade dos soldados.

Saving Private Ryan é um daqueles filmes que conseguem fazer a guerra parecer algo físico. Não é só assistir aos personagens lutando; existe uma sensação constante de caos, medo e desorientação. A sequência inicial do desembarque na Normandia é provavelmente uma das representações mais impactantes de combate que já vi. Spielberg não tenta transformar aquilo em uma batalha "bonita". A câmera fica próxima dos soldados, o som é agressivo e tudo acontece de maneira extremamente caótica. Também gosto bastante de como o filme equilibra as grandes cenas de batalha com momentos mais silenciosos entre os personagens. A missão de encontrar Ryan funciona como uma estrutura para discutir o custo humano da guerra e o significado de sacrificar algumas vidas para salvar uma pessoa. Tom Hanks funciona muito bem como Miller porque ele não é apresentado como um super-herói. É um homem tentando cumprir uma missão enquanto carrega o peso de tudo que está acontecendo ao redor. É um filme longo, mas a direção mantém a tensão muito bem construída. Um clássico do gênero e, pra mim, facilmente 5 estrelas.

“Earn this.” The famous final words of Tom Hanks’ Captain Miller as he dies on the bridge at the end of Saving Private Ryan. I don’t think we fully comprehend what we have when it comes to freedom in the United States. Captain Miller and his band of brothers embark on a mission to save just one soldier, and one by one, they sacrifice themselves to secure his freedom and his future. As Miller lies dying, his final words to Private Ryan are simple: “Earn this.” That phrase feels increasingly distant from the hearts and minds of Americans today. What are we supposed to earn? Most of us honestly don’t know. We have grown up surrounded by freedoms of every kind, so completely immersed in them that it can be difficult to imagine another reality—one in which those freedoms are absent, restricted, or taken away entirely. Freedom can never be treated as something guaranteed. It requires vigilance, but it also requires something more: responsibility toward one another. We inherit a country and a way of life purchased, time and time again, through the sacrifices of people we will never meet. I hope that, in brotherhood and sisterhood, we can continue striving to earn this—not because freedom should have to be earned as a condition of possessing it, but because sacrifice deserves remembrance, gratitude, and a willingness to leave something worthy behind for the generations that follow us. One of the greatest films ever made. In nearly every way, Saving Private Ryan is a masterpiece.

Saving Private Ryan is a phenomenal movie. I’ve been wanting to watch this film for a long time and this was one of the first films I ever put on my watchlist. I always wanted to watch this film because it seemed like the type of film I would love but for some reason I kept pushing it back. I decided it was finally time that I watched this iconic film and because of all the fantastic things I had read/heard about it I had extremely high expectations. All of my high expectations where exceeded, every single aspect of this film completely blew me away. Besides a few minor problems it’s honestly hard to think of any major or notable flaws. The plot is great it’s an immensely realistic and captivating story. The second the film starts it grabs your complete attention and doesn’t let go until the credits role. Right off the bat the story begins with a brutally intense and masterfully crafted 30 minutes depicting the events of D-Day. Those 30 are undoubtedly some of the most well made and truly heartbreaking moments in film history. The story is such a human story that brilliantly balances an array of moral themes. It’s the type of story where you can’t help but ponder what’s to happen next because of how unpredictably realistic the story can get. The pacing is great since it’s absolutely an engaging story there isn’t a single slow or boring moment. The acting is phenomenal Tom Hanks a phenomenal performance. Hanks doesn’t even have to try and give an outstanding performance he’s just that amazing of an actor. Matt Damon, Tom Sizemore, Edward Burns, Barry Pepper, Adam Goldberg, Vin Diesel, and Giovanni Ribisi give fantastic supporting performances as well. This film seriously has one of the most versatile and talented casts of all time. The direction is phenomenal from Steven Spielberg, every single one of his directorial choices felt masterfully thought out and genius. Spielberg truly knows how to tell an incredibly important story. The script is fantastic it’s an authentic and very well written script stacked with memorable pieces of dialogue between the platoon. The cinematography is phenomenal this film is full of beautiful and impressive shots that immerse the audience into WW2. The visual effects and editing are phenomenal as well. The score is phenomenal from John Williams he really knows how to make a score that strikes up personal emotion. I’ve said this many times before and I’ll say it again Williams is the greatest film composer of all time. It’s hard to believe that Shakespeare in Love won Best Picture, Best Original Screenplay, and Best Original Score won over this. The ending is a heartfelt ending that brings you close to tears. Overall Saving Private Ryan is an intensely realistic and overwhelmingly stunning war film that’s absolutely a true masterpiece.
